newsitem.title: USA: CSX sees continued rate pressure on Sea-Land.
newsitem.headline: CSX sees continued rate pressure on Sea-Land.

text.p: CSX Corp said it expects the pressure on its Sea-Land unit from low rates, which dragged on its 1996 earnings, to continue in the first half of 1997. But it sees strong profits ahead for the business when the cloud of low rates lifts.

"Rates will continue to be under pressure in at least the first half of 1997 but at some point that will ameliorate and ... you will begin to see the core earning power at Sea-Land. It's a lot higher," said Chairman John Snow at an earnings presentation on Thursday in New York.
Snow said that at the unit, "cost and expense reduction has become a religion". He cited as evidence higher operating profits of $318 million in the fourth quarter despite lower revenues.
Andrew Fogarty, chief financial officer of Sea-Land, said he expects strong gains in 1997 although he declined to set a specific numerical goal.
"We expect to have numbers that represent a very significant pickup over this year, Fogarty said.
When asked if the unit might beat a goal of $350 million in 1997 operating earnings, he said: "Our targets are higher than that."
For the year, Sea-Land had a 34 percent improvement operating earnings, said CSX Chief Financial Officer Paul Goodwin.

CSX's rail business CSX Transportation had 1996 operating earnings of $1.13 billion, or six percent above last year, "on traffic levels which where basically flat. Revenues were about two percent above last year and despite some $51 million in fuel prices," Goodwin said.
CSX's railroad business CSX Transportation and Sea-Land are the two principal units of CSX.
